q-73776.name: Question 1
q-73776.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{2}+5x+4?$

I. $x=4$ is a root of $f(x)$

II. $(x-4)$ is a factor of $f(x)$

III. $(x-4)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder
q-73776.worked_solution:
The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(x-4).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-4 & =0 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

We now check each of the statements, in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, $x=4$ is not a root of $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4) & ={4}^{2}+5(4)+4 \\  & =16+20+4 \\  & =40 \\  & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. According to the factor theorem, since $x=4$ is not a root of $f(x),$ then $(x-4)$ is not a factor of $f(x).$

- Statement III is false. Since $(x-4)$ is not a factor of $f(x),$ then it does not divide $f(x)$ with zero remainder.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None."

q-73777.name: Question 2
q-73777.problem:
For which of the following polynomials is $(x+1)$ a factor?

I. $f(x)={x}^{2}+3x+2$

II. $g(x)={x}^{2}+8x+7$

III. $h(x)=-{x}^{2}+x$
q-73777.worked_solution:
The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(x+1).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =0 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

According to the factor theorem, $(x+1)$ is a factor of $p(x)$ if the root $x=-1$ is a root of $p(x).$ 

So now, we will check if $x=-1$ is a root of the polynomials $f,$ $g$ and $h.$

- Evaluating $x=-1$ at $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1) & =(-1)^{2}+3(-1)+2 \\  & =1-3+2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that $(x+1)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$

- Now, evaluating $x=-1$ at $g(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-1) & =(-1)^{2}+8(-1)+7 \\  & =1-8+7 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that $(x+1)$ is indeed a factor of $g(x).$

- Finally, evaluating $x=-1$ at $h(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-1) & =-(-1)^{2}+(-1) \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

q-112375.name: Question 3
q-112375.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}-64?$

I. $x=-4$ is a root of $f(x)$

II. $(x+4)$ is a factor of $f(x)$

III. $(x+4)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder
q-112375.worked_solution:
The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(x+4).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4 & =0 \\ x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

We now check each of the statements, in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, $x=-4$ is not a root of $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-4) & =(-4)^{3}-64 \\  & =-64-64 \\  & =-128 \\  & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. According to the factor theorem, since $x=-4$ is not a root of $f(x),$ then $(x+4)$ is not a factor of $f(x).$

- Statement III is false. Since $(x+4)$ is not a factor of $f(x),$ then it does not divide $f(x)$ with zero remainder.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."
